title: Why are Wrestlers so FREAKY?
summary: A scripted essay on why wrestlers are so strong and muscular: the sport is itself resistance training that builds neck, traps, upper back and posterior chain, combined with brutal practice from early childhood and fast-paced functional lifting. Using Karelin and Dagestan as examples, NH concludes that consistency, replicating wrestling movement patterns in the gym (for example neck curls instead of bridges), and fierce drive are the lessons for lifters.
claims: As a kid he saw a small wrestler slam a 6 ft plus 14-year-old onto concrete in an instant
Wrestling itself is resistance training: every route to victory requires physically overpowering an opponent
Wrestlers' standout muscles are neck, traps, hamstrings, glutes and upper back, grown from the patterns they drill: hip-hinge stance, pushing and pulling arms, neck used as a fifth limb
Wrestling practices are among the most strenuous in sport for both cardio and nervous-system stress, and many start at age four or five
Wrestlers combine drilling with fast-paced, functional lifting sessions aimed at strength and explosiveness, not bodybuilding
Milo of Croton, the legendary wrestler who carried a calf daily until it became an ox, is the father of progressive overload
Weight cutting and starving limit anabolism, so wrestlers' physiques are impressive despite not training for hypertrophy
Karelin was 6'4 and about 290 lb with a 420 lb clean and press, a 22+ inch neck and 887 wins to 2 losses
NH believes Karelin had acromegaly or used GH, which does not erase his accomplishments since drugs are only half the answer
Environment matters: Dagestan's harsh culture plus wrestling produces a remarkable number of top fighters
Consistency is key: the best wrestlers have been at it longest, and the survival bias is one of willpower
Since physique reflects the movement patterns you train, you can get similar results by replicating them with resistance training without the technical demands
Neck curls instead of neck bridges build the neck without the risk
In the gym you are your own opponent; adversity and a fire to train harder are what most recreational lifters lack
exercises: safer than neck bridges for neck growth
